answers.text: The instruction should return exactly three lines every time, in this order: delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order. If a field is missing from the email, I'd have it note 'not stated' rather than drop the line.
List every claim by date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amounts at the bottom. If two lines look like duplicates of the same claim, I'd flag it rather than add both in.
The delivery date doesn't match the stated gap — 'three days out' from the 14th should be the 17th, not the 19th. I'd confirm the real call date against the call log before this goes out.
62 up from 54 is correctly about 15%. But 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not the 97% quoted — I'd flag that.
Output 2, because it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 could still be correct, but there's no way to verify it without re-running the calculation yourself.
Reply 2 — the order reference and credit reference make it checkable. Reply 1 might well be accurate, I'd just want to see it backed by something before sending it.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. Yes, it's already published on the website. 5. No.
The unit pricing and volume discounts I'd redact, and the confidentiality clause needs care too since it names both companies directly.
Before the report reaches the manager, I'd cross-check the delivery and stock totals against the warehouse system.
Step 1's extraction carries risk downstream, but step 4 — the automatic confirmation — is where the real gate belongs, checking the stock figure is genuinely current before it's sent.
